title: Marcus Aurelius Auctions the Palace Treasures
text:
In the late 160s the Roman Empire was in crisis. A plague brought back by the army from the east was killing large numbers of people, and Germanic peoples were crossing the Danube frontier. The emperor Marcus Aurelius needed money for a long war, and the treasury was empty.

According to the Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies written later, Marcus refused to impose new taxes on the provinces. Instead he held a public auction in the Forum of Trajan in Rome. He sold the imperial furnishings: gold and crystal cups, vessels fit for kings, statues and paintings by great artists, and even his wife's silk and gold-embroidered robes and the jewels he found in a private treasury of the emperor Hadrian. The sale went on for two months, the biography says.

It raised enough to carry on the war. Afterward, the biography adds, Marcus let it be known that anyone who wished to return what they had bought could do so and get the price back, but he did not pressure those who chose to keep their purchases. The historian Eutropius tells the same story.
lesson: Before asking others to give something up, give up something of your own first. People notice who pays.
source: Historia Augusta, Life of Marcus Aurelius, chapters 17 and 21; Eutropius, Breviarium, Book 8, chapter 13
caveat: The Historia Augusta is often unreliable, though Eutropius independently reports the auction.
